title: German Occupation Administration Takes Shape
subtitle: From military conquest to civilian rule
body:
A government for conquest

On October 26, 1939, Hans Frank ordered the Polish population of the General Government to carry identity cards recording such details as descent, religion, occupation, and state affiliation, together with a fingerprint. The directive did not put a card into every hand that morning. It claimed the power to classify the inhabitants of a conquered country and entrusted implementation to the Higher SS and Police Leader. Alongside new labour and publishing regulations, it shows what the administrative change meant: German authority would reach repeatedly into ordinary life, long after the invading columns had passed. [6] Western and northern territories were being annexed to the Reich; Frank took charge of the separate General Government in the remaining German-occupied area. [1] The [September 28 treaty](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28) had allocated the occupiers’ territories. October brought decisions about the institutions that would administer Germany’s share. Their purpose included exploitation, demographic change, and the suppression of independent Polish leadership. Those aims could compete: expelling workers could interrupt production, while confiscating a factory did not by itself keep it running. The emerging system gave several agencies authority over the same people and resources. Its conflicts concerned how to carry out domination, not whether the occupied population should regain control of its affairs. [2] [3] a Three decrees supplied the framework. Hitler’s October 7 decree on strengthening German nationhood—*Festigung deutschen Volkstums*—gave Heinrich Himmler responsibility for bringing ethnic Germans into the Reich’s orbit, establishing settlements, and eliminating the influence of populations defined as threatening to German interests. The decree combined resettlement with coercion from its inception: Himmler could take general and administrative measures to carry out that racial program. Its categories expressed Nazi ideology, not objective differences in people’s entitlement to live in their own country. [4] Hitler’s decree of October 8 concerned the organization and administration of eastern territories to be incorporated into Germany. The decree bearing the date October 12 placed the remaining occupied Polish territories under a governor general, appointed Frank, and made him directly subordinate to Hitler. Both arrangements took effect on October 26, after further decisions about the changeover. The dates printed on the founding instruments were therefore different from the date on which the new civilian administrations formally assumed authority. [5] [6] b

Synchronizing the occupation

An effective date brought forward

The annexation decree initially specified November 1, 1939. A further decree on October 20 advanced its operation to October 26, bringing it into line with the General Government’s administrative changeover. Pospieszalski identifies both the amendment and the need to avoid leaving the incorporated territories under military administration after the neighbouring civilian system had begun. The adjustment reveals coordination between legal instruments that a single anniversary date tends to conceal. c

[5]

Reading the legal record

The disputed signature date

Legal historian Karol Marian Pospieszalski argued, from Frank’s recollections and the surrounding decisions, that the decree bearing the date October 12 was actually signed later, probably around October 19. That is a reconstruction of its preparation, distinct from the date printed on the instrument. Its effective date, October 26, remains the relevant administrative turning point here. The distinction illustrates why publication, signature and implementation should not automatically be treated as a single event. d

[5]

Choosing the territory—and changing its population

The annexed lands did not form one uniform province. The October settlement created Reichsgaue, territorial units combining state administration with Nazi Party power, at West Prussia and Posen. The former became Danzig–West Prussia on November 2; the latter received the name Wartheland on January 29, 1940. Those familiar later names can obscure the sequence. Posen, centred on Poznań, was governed by Arthur Greiser; Albert Forster headed the northern unit, which brought together the former Free City of Danzig, much of Polish Pomerania and the Corridor, and territory previously administered within German East Prussia. [7] Danzig requires a qualification. Before the war, it was a Free City under League of Nations protection, with specified Polish rights; it was not simply another province of the Polish Republic. German incorporation of Danzig and annexation of sovereign Polish territory were therefore distinct acts, even when the occupation subsequently placed them within the same administrative unit. Elsewhere, Germany enlarged existing provinces. The Ciechanów region went into East Prussia, while Polish Upper Silesia, including Katowice, was attached to Silesia. Describing every annexed district as part of either Posen or Danzig–West Prussia would erase these important differences. [8] [1] Łódź initially remained in the General Government. Sylwia Grochowina’s chronology places its incorporation into the Reich on November 9, after the October changeover. The later German name Litzmannstadt also belongs to a later moment: the city was renamed on April 11, 1940. The enlarged annexed territory reached beyond Germany’s pre-1914 frontier. Incorporation was being used to expand German rule and reorganize the lives of people the occupiers intended to subordinate or displace; it cannot be explained simply as the reversal of the Versailles settlement. [7] [9] [10] e The German division also did not encompass every territorial adjustment arising from the invasion. Slovakia had participated in the September attack, but its formal agreement with Germany transferring disputed Polish border districts was concluded on **November 21**. That later act should not be folded into the German administrative settlement of October 26. It belonged to a separate bilateral arrangement involving Spisz and Orawa, regions where border disputes had preceded the war. Distinguishing the agreements identifies which government asserted authority, over which places, and at what stage. [11] f Annexation brought productive farmland and industrial regions into the Reich, including Polish Upper Silesia. Göring’s instructions of October 19 distinguished how these resources were to be treated. In incorporated areas, productive capacity and supplies were to be preserved and developed within the German economy. From the General Government, he demanded the removal of useful raw materials, machinery, and enterprises. This difference assigned the territories contrasting economic functions without granting either population a voice in the disposition of its property or work. [7] [3] Racial policy gave annexation a demographic purpose. Himmler’s mandate treated resettlement and the assignment of new living areas as tasks of state, subordinating existing residence and Polish citizenship to categories defined by the regime. The aim was to transform the population, rather than simply recognize an existing territorial condition. Benefits offered to arriving ethnic Germans were consequently connected to the removal and dispossession of other inhabitants. Although later procedures and the scale of deportation were still developing, the link between settlement and coercion was already embedded in the authority granted on October 7. [4] This also helps explain why Germany did not annex everything it occupied. In the record of Hitler’s October 17 conference with Wilhelm Keitel, the remaining Polish territory was assigned a low standard of living, a supply of labour, and a military role. Roads, railways, and communications were to remain useful to Germany, while the emergence of an independent Polish leadership was to be prevented. The area would also receive people removed from the Reich. Keeping it outside direct incorporation allowed the regime to exploit and police its inhabitants without undertaking to absorb them into the national community it claimed to be constructing. This was a deliberate allocation of functions, although particular borders and practices remained subject to argument. [2] g

Frank’s authority, and its limits

The General Government began with four districts: Kraków, Warsaw, Radom, and Lublin. Galicia was added only in 1941. Frank, a lawyer and longstanding Nazi, presided over an administration in which German district heads and subordinate officials exercised authority over occupied communities. The October 26 organizational ordinance designated Kraków as his official seat. This was a German governmental decision, not a transfer of the Polish Republic’s capital: Warsaw’s reduced place in the occupation hierarchy did not make it cease to be Poland’s capital in Polish political life. [1] [6] Frank’s government was still taking physical shape. Although the organizational ordinance designated Kraków as his seat, he initially worked from Łódź and formally moved to Kraków on November 7. Pospieszalski’s reconstruction follows disputes over which territory would remain in the General Government, including the industrial and urban assets that officials wanted under their jurisdiction. The new administration’s founding did not end that competition. Offices, revenues, and transport connections remained at stake in decisions made after October 26. [5] h The founding decree conferred extensive authority on Frank, but also contained the seeds of competing claims. He answered directly to Hitler and was assigned all branches of administration. Yet the Council of Ministers for the Defence of the Reich and Göring, as plenipotentiary for the Four-Year Plan, could also legislate for the territory. Reich authorities retained powers connected with wider German economic planning; the finance minister had to approve Frank’s budget, and the occupied territory itself was to bear the costs of administration. Frank’s government thus possessed a separate administrative identity without acquiring sovereign independence. Its inhabitants were expected to finance the machinery imposed on them. [6] Police authority created overlapping chains of command. Frank’s security ordinance of October 26 required the Higher SS and Police Leader to obtain Frank’s consent on matters of fundamental importance. Otherwise, the official could act independently and issue police regulations. The SS hierarchy also connected that official to Himmler. This distribution of powers complicated civilian control without making Frank an opponent of repression: his own ordinance authorized the coercive machinery. Jurisdictional conflict must therefore be examined as a feature of the occupation’s operation, rather than as evidence that its administrators stood outside the system’s violence. [6] [12] i The army’s withdrawal from general administration did not signify the end of military interests or a transition from violence to restraint. Hitler’s October 17 conference explicitly preserved the territory’s strategic importance, including the maintenance of communications for military use. The same record instructed the administration to prevent Polish political consolidation and denied that familiar legal restrictions should impede its racial objectives. Here the contrast with Hitler’s October 6 public speech is especially revealing. Before the Reichstag he had advertised peace, restored economic life, and the possible formation of a restricted Polish state; in the internal discussion, subsistence, labour extraction, and the suppression of leadership defined the assignment. [2] [13] The term “independence” in the October 17 conference record exposes the emptiness of the projected Polish political status. Hitler wanted the remaining territory kept outside the Reich while denying its inhabitants the means to develop their own leadership. The General Government subsequently created answered to him. Its separate accounts and offices did not amount to Polish self-government. This distinction mattered to those still working in local institutions: retaining a post or performing a public service no longer meant acting within the authority of their own state. [13] [2] j

Occupation at the counter, the workplace, and the school

The new order retained selected Polish institutions while placing them under German control. Section 4 of the founding decree preserved existing law only where it did not conflict with Germany’s assumption of administration. A separate ordinance of October 26 provided for German and Polish jurisdictions. It reserved protection of German security and prestige, and the lives, health and property of Germans, to German courts and allowed a German judge to review a final Polish judgment, set it aside, and transfer the case to German jurisdiction. Even a completed proceeding could thus be reopened by the occupying authority. The same ordinance deferred the courts’ activity until the General Government’s boundaries were finally established: authority was prescribed before the system was fully operating. [6] The preservation of selected municipal functions followed the same logic. Local records, finances and services required personnel and administrative continuity; the ordinance of November 28 subsequently made mayors accountable to occupation authorities who controlled appointment and supervision. A Polish official’s continued presence could therefore conceal a fundamental change in the authority exercised through the office. Assessing individual conduct requires further distinctions between maintaining essential services, responding to coercion and assisting persecution. The institution’s subordination establishes the setting in which those actions occurred, without determining every official’s motives or behaviour. [6] k The identity-card requirement placed this hierarchy at the level of the individual. Its recorded categories, including descent and religion, were categories through which the regime distinguished people’s treatment. The ordinance delegated the rules of implementation to the SS and police leader. An instruction to register the population was therefore also a grant of administrative power to a coercive institution. It must be read as an order, not as proof of universal registration on October 26; the timing and experience of obtaining documents require local evidence. [6] Labour regulations made unequal treatment explicit. The October 26 ordinance imposed a public labour obligation on Polish inhabitants aged eighteen to sixty, while providing separate rules for Jews. It specified agricultural work, public construction, transport infrastructure, and land improvement; people able to demonstrate continuing socially useful employment were not supposed to be called up under this particular obligation. Such qualifications did not make the system voluntary. They show how an administration could claim the power to allocate labour while distinguishing between those it considered already usefully employed and those it intended to direct elsewhere. [6] The parallel decree for Jews introduced compulsory labour and envisaged forced-labour groups, with implementation assigned to the SS and police leader. These were two differently organized mechanisms, issued on the same date. Polish Jews were citizens of the same republic, but Nazi administration separated them through racial categories and subjected them to additional persecution. Later measures widened the machinery: on December 14, district authorities received permission to extend the general Polish labour obligation to fourteen-to-eighteen-year-olds. That later extension should not be substituted for the original October age range. [6] l Developments immediately after the changeover reveal the educational purpose of the new authority. On October 31, Frank ordered Polish elementary and vocational schools to reopen, while requiring German and Polish children to attend separate schools. German schools were to employ German teachers; Polish private schools needed permission, and higher education was reserved for further regulation. On November 6, German security police arrested Kraków academics summoned to hear an official’s address. These later events are consequences of the emerging occupation, not measures already completed on October 26. They show how reopening some classrooms could coexist with an assault on independent intellectual life. [6] [14] An ordinance of October 26 also subjected publication, printing and distribution to permission, covering periodical and non-periodical material. The requirement placed the means of public communication under an administration committed to preventing independent Polish political organization. Its reach extended beyond newspapers to publishers, teachers, associations and religious activity that depended on printed material. Censorship thus operated through routine decisions about authorization as well as through seizures and violence. The bureaucratic procedure supplied a continuing means to restrict national and communal life after the immediate military conquest. [6] [2] m

Property, displacement, and terror

Göring’s October 19 economic instructions illuminate what administrative “order” meant for property. He demanded centralized custody of assets taken from Polish hands through the Main Trustee Office East, the *Haupttreuhandstelle Ost*, and described arrangements for state property and private Polish and Jewish property. The office could appoint administrators and replace ones installed by other agencies. Local confiscations were subject to confirmation. Göring condemned unauthorized seizures and private enrichment, but the purpose was to secure the proceeds for the Reich. Regulating confiscation did not restore the owners’ rights; it established which German institution should control what had been taken. [3] Göring’s instructions acknowledged that the newly divided territories had formed a connected economy, and claimed direction from Berlin despite their different administrative treatment. His demand to remove useful machinery from the General Government included a practical exception: where transfer would take too long, enterprises could fulfil German orders in place. The exception explains how preservation of production could accompany dispossession. It sustained output useful to the Reich without restoring the rights of the owners or workers. Economic continuity was therefore selective, determined by the occupier’s assessment of value and the constraints on extracting it. [3] n In Gdynia, the connection between racial policy and dispossession was already visible. The expulsions began in Orłowo on October 12. Monika Tomkiewicz records another removal from Kolonia–Obłuże on October 26, directed against residents categorized as coming from the former Congress Kingdom. Families were ordered to leave homes open with the keys in the doors and could take only hand luggage; furniture and household equipment had to remain. On the day civilian administration formally changed, the occupation was already deciding who could remain in a home and who would inherit its contents. [16] The IPN investigation into Gdynia’s deportations likewise identifies the October expulsions as part of German persecution of the city’s Polish inhabitants. [15] o Killing accompanied the construction of this system. German SS, police, military units, and the *Selbstschutz*, a paramilitary organization recruited among ethnic Germans, participated in the persecution of Polish civilians. The Holocaust Memorial Museum’s photograph record identifies a group about to be executed near Szubin on October 21, with an SD officer reading charges and a German soldier visible. The museum dates the execution photographs from Fordon to October–November and the Tuchola photograph to October 27. In the latter image, civilians are forced to dig a mass grave under SS and Selbstschutz guard. These records establish particular acts and settings; they do not supply a complete casualty total or identify every participant. They show terror continuing across the formal transition to civilian rule. [17] p The persecution also encompassed psychiatric patients. A later Polish investigation placed the removal and murder of patients from Owińska in the period from mid-October through November 1939. It found that early groups were killed with carbon monoxide in a sealed bunker at Fort VII in Poznań by Herbert Lange’s SS detachment. These are investigative findings based on testimony, including that of prisoners forced to remove the bodies. The precise chronology remains unresolved: the investigation could not establish exact dates, while a later IPN account dates the gassings to November. The evidence establishes the crime but does not justify assigning its completion, or a victim total, to October 26. [31] [32] q Anti-Jewish administration was developing through instructions that predated Frank’s government. On **September 21**, Reinhard Heydrich directed security-police commanders to concentrate Jewish populations in selected towns, favoring railway connections, and to establish Jewish councils whose members would be held responsible for carrying out German demands. Census-taking, accommodation and transport were made administrative tasks under coercion. Economic usefulness could delay removal: the instructions allowed enterprises needed for German purposes to keep operating temporarily. Such exceptions protected the occupier’s interests, not the owners’ rights. [18] These instructions should not be paraphrased as a universal order to establish sealed ghettos immediately. They set a direction of concentration and control while leaving implementation to develop unevenly. The first ghetto in occupied Poland was established at **Piotrków Trybunalski in October 1939**; other localities followed different timetables. Jewish councils, or *Judenräte*, were therefore emerging within a system of compulsory mediation: German authorities imposed responsibilities on community representatives while retaining coercive power over both representatives and those they were required to administer. The distinction between an instruction and its local execution helps explain why the same month could bring different restrictions to different towns. [19] [18] r The autumn campaign against Polish elites, commonly associated with the *Intelligenzaktion*, must be distinguished from the AB-Aktion of spring 1940. Auschwitz was also a later development, not a camp already operating at this October changeover. For Jews, humiliation, forced labour, dispossession, and expulsion were already realities, but the later extermination system cannot be projected backward as an institution fully formed in 1939. The General Government’s general armband decree was issued on November 23 and took effect on December 1, although local badge requirements had appeared earlier. These distinctions do not diminish the crimes already committed. They make it possible to identify the decisions through which persecution expanded. [20] [16] [21] [6] s

A resident’s recollection

Covering the windows in Gdynia

Jadwiga Kocuniak later recalled sheltering with her family in a friend’s building on Świętojańska Street when German troops entered Gdynia. Soldiers shouted orders to cover the windows and not look out, threatening to shoot. Preserved in Monika Tomkiewicz’s account, the recollection concerns the occupation’s first days, before October’s administrative settlement. It conveys the immediate coercion behind the official language of restored order. [16] t

Polish continuity under occupation

Displacement damaged the connections through which people normally obtained safety: home, relatives, employment, and neighbours. Refugees who tried to return from the Soviet zone were acting within this damaged social world. The [boundary study](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28) examines their journeys; here their importance is the dependence that occupation created. A formal administrative division could separate a person from shelter or livelihood while officials on either side claimed the power to decide whether a crossing was permitted. [22] u Abroad, the Polish government under President Władysław Raczkiewicz and Prime Minister Władysław Sikorski continued to reject the partition. Potocki’s September 30 protest remained directly relevant as German decrees purported to dispose of Polish territory and institutions. This was not acceptance of a reduced Polish government under Frank. The recognized government operated in France, while the occupying administration exercised coercive power at home. [23] [24] Inside occupied Poland, organized resistance was also beginning to take institutional form. On September 27, General Michał Tokarzewski-Karaszewicz began building *Służba Zwycięstwu Polski*, the Service for Poland’s Victory. The organization represented an early attempt to sustain coordinated struggle after the collapse of open military defence. It was not yet the Home Army. Sikorski created the Union of Armed Struggle in November 1939. It took over the earlier organization’s structures and was renamed the Home Army in February 1942. Keeping these stages separate preserves something important about October: clandestine structures had to be built under conditions of uncertainty, surveillance, and repression, rather than simply continuing as an already complete underground state. [23] [33] v

Moscow’s parallel settlement, and the Western refusal

In eastern Poland, Soviet authorities sought to present absorption into the USSR as a popular decision. Controlled elections on October 22 produced assemblies selected for that purpose. The Western Ukrainian assembly convened in Lwów, now Lviv, on October 26–28; the Western Belarusian assembly met in Białystok later that month. The USSR’s Supreme Soviet approved the incorporation of Western Ukraine on November 1 and Western Belarus on November 2. On October 26, therefore, German civilian administration was formally beginning while Soviet occupation was still being converted into a claim of annexation. These were distinct processes, not simultaneous versions of one legal act. [25] [26] The Western Ukrainian assembly’s declaration on October 27 claimed unanimous popular support for Soviet power. Its wording belongs to the occupation’s public case, not to independent evidence of consent. During the subsequent consolidation of Soviet rule, the extension of its institutions also brought action against private enterprise, political organizations, and religious life, enforced through the NKVD, the Soviet internal-affairs apparatus that included the political police. Jewish inhabitants could escape Nazi racial persecution and still face Soviet coercion. Neither that immediate escape nor support from some individuals can be made into consent on behalf of an entire community. [27] [28] w Cooperation between Berlin and Moscow continued alongside these different programs. Steinhardt’s October 9 report recorded German economic negotiators in Moscow, including agricultural and railway representatives, and the head of the German frontier commission. The significance here is practical: the territorial bargain needed transport arrangements, officials, and working contacts. Those negotiations supported the consolidation of conquest even while the two governments organized their respective zones differently. The boundary-treaty study examines the related trade and transit commitments. [29] [24] x Britain and France refused to accept conquest as a sufficient basis for peace. Chamberlain’s October 12 statement rejected the freedom Hitler claimed to dispose of conquered peoples and cited Daladier’s insistence on dependable security. Hull’s October 2 statement separately affirmed continued American recognition of Poland; it survives here through its reproduction in a 1945 briefing paper. These positions denied the political finality the occupiers sought. They did not stop Frank’s decrees, Soviet incorporation proceedings, or the police forces enforcing occupation. [30] [10] y

The institutions of domination

The October settlement made coercion more durable by assigning offices the power to repeat it. A police commander could enforce a registration requirement; a labour office could call up workers; a German judge could overturn a Polish judgment; a trustee could take control of property. These were specific mechanisms through which the occupier displaced the protections of Polish citizenship. Rivalry among German agencies might change which official made a decision without restoring the inhabitant’s right to determine it. [3] [6] The people subjected to this administration had already endured invasion, killing, and flight. October added procedures that could turn an assault on a family or community into an enduring condition: loss of a home, loss of employment, compulsory work, censorship, or detention. The chronology remains essential. Later ghettos, deportation campaigns, and killing systems grew through further decisions; their subsequent scale must not erase what had already been done or make their development appear automatic. [17] [15] By the end of this collection, the two invasions had destroyed Poland’s ability to defend its territory through conventional operations. German and Soviet authorities were replacing its institutions according to different political and ideological programs. Polish government abroad and resistance at home preserved the struggle for independence, but offered uneven and often inadequate protection to people living under occupation. The partition’s meaning lay in this imbalance: a state continued to claim its people and territory while foreign officials acquired the power to govern, dispossess, imprison, and kill within them. [24] [10] [23]
author: Robert M. Dobo
location: German-occupied Poland, with responses from Moscow and the Western capitals
summary: Annexation and the General Government gave German conquest different administrative forms. Decrees concerning property, labour, policing and local authority brought the occupiers’ power into daily life while the recognized Polish government continued abroad.

sourceMethod: The study centres on October 26, 1939, distinguishes earlier preparation from the administrative changeover, and explicitly dates brief later consequences. German decrees are paraphrased from the original German transcriptions in Documenta Occupationis VI; its English introductory analysis is distinguished from the documents. The October 17 Hitler–Keitel conference record, October 7 Himmler decree, and October 19 Göring instructions establish stated policy, not uniform implementation. Local research and museum records supply evidence of expulsions and killings. Selected scholarly pages, not whole volumes, were consulted. Daladier’s October 10 broadcast is accessed through Chamberlain’s October 12 statement; Hull’s October 2 statement through a 1945 documentary reproduction. Source access and unresolved precision limits are recorded in the accompanying editorial review.
